rationale: Start with a broad scouting gradient to locate all six peaks and identify critical pairs while limiting late-elution penalties. Use a midrange temperature so subsequent runs can probe selectivity in either direction.

The first method already achieves the maximum CRF, with ample resolution margin. Shorten the gradient at unchanged temperature and endpoints to seek a faster fully resolved method and measure how the closest pair responds to slope.

Shorten the gradient one grid step while keeping temperature and endpoints fixed. The closest pair's slope response suggests resolution may remain above 1.5, yielding a faster method with the same maximum CRF.

The 4-minute gradient retains maximum CRF but leaves little resolution margin for the first pair. Test higher temperature at unchanged gradient to shorten retention and determine whether temperature improves or erodes that pair's selectivity.

Higher temperature compressed the critical first pair, so test the lowest temperature to improve its selectivity while shortening the gradient to the minimum duration. This probes whether cooling can preserve full resolution in a faster run; injection 3 remains the proven fast method.

Narrow the gradient span to reduce steepness and lift the first pair's resolution toward 1.5 while retaining the 2-minute gradient. The last peak will likely elute during the final hold, so this run tests whether full resolution can be achieved without sacrificing the time advantage.

Shift the gradient window upward while preserving the slope that fully resolved injection 6. The higher endpoint should accelerate the last peak substantially; this tests whether the first pair retains sufficient resolution at the higher starting organic fraction.

Shift the window upward another 0.10 at the same slope and temperature to accelerate the final peak. Injection 7 preserved the critical pair's resolution; this run tests whether that margin survives as the early peaks approach the gradient front.

Raise the starting organic fraction one step to shorten retention while slightly reducing gradient steepness. Monitor the first pair closely because its peaks are approaching the unretained region, despite the potential resolution benefit of the shallower slope.

Raise temperature one step to accelerate the final peak while testing the first pair's remaining resolution margin. Keep the starting organic fraction unchanged because the earliest peak is already close to the gradient front.

Test one higher starting organic fraction to see whether the shallower gradient preserves the first pair's resolution while shortening the final retention time. This deliberately probes the early-elution boundary; injection 10 remains the fastest proven maximum-CRF method.

Return to the starting fraction that retained the first pair and test the next temperature step to establish the thermal resolution boundary. This may shorten the run further, although the first pair's trend suggests its resolution could fall below 1.5.

Reduce the gradient span to recover the first pair's resolution at 35 C; the slope change should bring its R back above 1.5. This tests an alternative fully resolved operating window while measuring the late-peak hold penalty from the lower endpoint.

The first pair barely responded to slope at phi0 0.30, suggesting it is too close to the gradient front. Shift the window downward at unchanged slope to retain that pair longer and test whether its resolution recovers; the last peak should still elute well within 10 minutes.

Cooling one step should improve the critical pair's selectivity enough to permit a higher endpoint and faster final-peak elution than injection 14. The lower starting fraction also keeps the first pair away from the near-unretained regime seen at phi0 0.35.

Test whether cooling restores the early-pair resolution lost at this starting fraction at 30 C. This completes the nearby high-organic boundary check while retaining the fastest proven maximum-CRF method from injection 10 as the fallback.

The higher starting fraction failed even at 25 C, so return to phi0 0.30 and slightly reduce the endpoint to improve the critical pair's resolution margin. This seeks a more robust maximum-CRF alternative with only a small retention-time increase over injection 10.

Raise temperature one step from injection 17 to shorten the final hold while testing whether its added resolution margin is retained. This refines a fast maximum-CRF alternative near the fastest proven method, injection 10.

The maximum CRF is already secured, so test a fast alternative with more resolution margin and better early-peak retention. Relative to injection 8, lowering the endpoint should spread the critical pair while keeping the last peak comfortably within 10 minutes.

Raise the endpoint one step from injection 19 to shorten the final peak's hold while preserving useful resolution margin. This refines the compromise between early-peak retention, full resolution, and speed; injection 10 remains the fastest proven maximum-CRF method.

Raise temperature one step from injection 19 to shorten late elution while retaining the lower starting fraction and its better early-peak retention. The observed temperature response suggests the critical pair should remain above 1.5, providing another fast maximum-CRF operating point.

Test the remaining high-endpoint neighbor of the fastest proven method to determine whether lower starting organic can preserve full resolution at comparable speed. The first pair may fall just below 1.5, so injection 10 remains the established maximum-CRF fallback.

Shift injection 8's fully resolved gradient window downward by 0.05 at unchanged slope and temperature to improve early-peak retention. This tests a nearby maximum-CRF alternative with modestly longer late retention, while injection 10 remains the fastest proven method.

Raise the endpoint one step from injection 23 to shorten late elution and test whether its first-pair resolution margin survives the steeper gradient. This probes the full-resolution boundary at a lower starting fraction; injection 10 remains the fastest proven maximum-CRF method.

Use the final injection to test a nearby method expected to retain maximum CRF with more first-pair resolution margin than injection 24. Injection 10 remains the fastest proven fully resolved method, with the last peak at 2.58 minutes.
